sections.title: To ALEXANDER GRAHAM BELL
sections.routing_description: Helen dedicates her life story to Alexander Graham Bell for his work with speech and hearing.

sections.title: Editor's Preface
sections.routing_description: John Albert Macy explains the three-part book, his editorial responsibility, and the friends and publishers who supplied letters and records.

sections.title: CHAPTER I
sections.routing_description: Helen recounts her family origins, childhood home and garden, and the illness at nineteen months that took her sight and hearing.

sections.title: CHAPTER II
sections.routing_description: Helen describes childhood signs and mischief with Martha Washington, her family, and her early jealousy of her sister Mildred.

sections.title: CHAPTER III
sections.routing_description: As signs become inadequate, Helen’s parents seek help from Dr. Chisholm and Alexander Graham Bell, leading them to Perkins and a teacher.

sections.title: CHAPTER IV
sections.routing_description: Anne Sullivan arrives, teaches finger spelling, and helps Helen connect the word water with the stream at the well-house. Helen then regrets breaking her doll.

sections.title: CHAPTER V
sections.routing_description: Helen learns about nature, is frightened by a thunderstorm while waiting in a tree, and later overcomes her fear by climbing a flowering mimosa.

sections.title: CHAPTER VI
sections.routing_description: Helen learns the abstract meanings of think and love. She explains how Sullivan uses conversation spelled into her hand to teach language.

sections.title: CHAPTER VII
sections.routing_description: Raised-letter slips lead Helen to reading. Sullivan teaches geography, natural science, and other lessons through outdoor play, objects, stories, and observation.

sections.title: CHAPTER VIII
sections.routing_description: Helen enjoys preparing and receiving Christmas surprises, then cares for her canary Little Tim until a cat takes him.

sections.title: CHAPTER IX
sections.routing_description: Helen visits Boston and Perkins, communicates directly with blind children, and explores Bunker Hill, Plymouth, and the Endicotts’ home.

sections.title: CHAPTER X
sections.routing_description: At Brewster Helen first enters the ocean, is overwhelmed by waves, and later catches a horseshoe crab that escapes from its trough.
retrieval_cues: Who put salt in the water

sections.title: CHAPTER XI
sections.routing_description: Helen recalls hunting gatherings and riding at Fern Quarry, then describes escaping a train with Mildred and Sullivan while crossing a trestle.

sections.title: CHAPTER XII
sections.routing_description: Helen experiences a New England winter, a snowstorm that isolates the household, and the exhilaration of tobogganing over a frozen lake.

sections.title: CHAPTER XIII
sections.routing_description: Inspired by Ragnhild Kaata, Helen begins speech lessons with Sarah Fuller, practises with Sullivan, and returns home able to speak to her family.

sections.title: CHAPTER XIV
sections.routing_description: Helen recounts the plagiarism accusation over The Frost King, the investigation at Perkins, and her lasting uncertainty about memory, imitation, and original writing.

sections.title: CHAPTER XV
sections.routing_description: Sullivan encourages Helen to write an account of her life. Helen describes Niagara and exploring exhibits at the World’s Fair with Alexander Graham Bell.

sections.title: CHAPTER XVI
sections.routing_description: Helen moves from informal French and history study to scheduled lessons with Mr. Irons in Latin, arithmetic, and critical reading.

sections.title: CHAPTER XVII
sections.routing_description: Helen attends Wright-Humason in New York, studies languages and geography while struggling with speech and arithmetic, and mourns John P. Spaulding.

sections.title: CHAPTER XVIII
sections.routing_description: Helen prepares for Radcliffe at the Cambridge School, shares lessons and recreation with other girls, and passes preliminary examinations with Gilman interpreting.

sections.title: CHAPTER XIX
sections.routing_description: Access problems and a disagreement about Helen’s workload lead her to leave Cambridge School. Tutoring with Merton Keith prepares her for finals complicated by unfamiliar braille notation.

sections.title: CHAPTER XX
sections.routing_description: Helen describes studying at Radcliffe, using a Hammond typewriter and interpreted lectures, and weighs the pleasures of literature against cramming, examinations, and lack of reflection time.

sections.title: CHAPTER XXI
sections.routing_description: Helen traces her reading from embossed beginners’ books and Little Lord Fauntleroy to classical poetry, the Bible, Shakespeare, history, and European literature, explaining her preferences.

sections.title: CHAPTER XXII
sections.routing_description: Helen describes rowing, sailing, country walks, adapted games, sculpture, and theatre, including a storm at Halifax and actors who let her follow performances by touch.

sections.title: CHAPTER XXIII
sections.routing_description: Helen recalls friendships with religious teachers, writers, inventors, and benefactors, including visits to Holmes and Whittier and Bell’s kite experiments.

sections.title: CHAPTER I. The Writing of the Book
sections.routing_description: John Albert Macy explains how Keller composed and revised her autobiography using a typewriter, braille manuscripts, and Sullivan's assistance. He distinguishes reconstructed childhood memories from teaching records and describes her editorial independence.

sections.title: CHAPTER II. PERSONALITY
sections.routing_description: Macy describes Keller's humour, persistence, friendships, reasoning, and daily habits. He examines her use of touch, smell, music, the manual alphabet, braille, a typewriter, and adapted watches, and disputes claims of a mysterious extra sense.
locations: Museum of Fine Arts in Boston

sections.title: CHAPTER III. EDUCATION
sections.routing_description: John Albert Macy traces Samuel Gridley Howe’s work with Laura Bridgman, then presents Anne Sullivan’s early letters and educational reports on Helen Keller. These document discipline in the garden-house, the water-pump naming breakthrough, language learned through everyday conversation and books, sensory observations, and questions about birth, death and religion; Macy closes by assessing Sullivan’s teaching principles and Keller’s abilities.

sections.title: CHAPTER IV. SPEECH
sections.routing_description: Macy assesses Keller's voice and pronunciation. Sullivan recounts her early sounds, determination to speak, Sarah Fuller's lessons, and continued practice; Keller's 1896 Mount Airy address explains the personal value of spoken communication.

sections.title: CHAPTER V. LITERARY STYLE
sections.routing_description: Macy traces Keller's literary style through reading, revision, and college composition. Documents and parallel stories examine the Frost King controversy and remembered language; excerpts from her early autobiography, essays, Horace translation, and accounts of dreams illustrate her writing.
